title: Materials: what they are like, and why we test them
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers NCERT Class 3 'This World of Things' (what things are made of, where they come from, natural and made by people, properties of materials) and Cambridge Stage 3 Chemistry: Unit 5.1 'Properties of materials', Unit 5.2 'Sorting materials', Unit 5.3 'Uses of materials' and Unit 5.4 'Testing materials'. No textbook needed.
summary: A steel spoon sticks to a magnet, but many steel tumblers do not. Your child learns to test materials instead of guessing. They sort things as transparent, translucent or opaque, find out what metals have in common and which ones are magnetic, and tell solids, liquids and gases apart. They build a branching key, repeat a measured test to see if it is reliable, and peel pencil graphite thinner and thinner with sticky tape. They find out why the moon suit needed about twenty layers, and why old glass does not flow.
builds_on: Class 1: object and material, simple property words, simple tests. Class 2: natural and made materials and their journeys, rigid, flexible, absorbent, waterproof, transparent, fair tests with tables and block graphs, biodegradable. Next: Changing materials (Class 4) and Matter and particles (Class 4) explain why materials have their properties. Making things (Classes 3 to 5) uses them.
subconcepts: metals: shiny, ring when struck, carry heat, often strong
magnetic and non-magnetic materials: only some metals are magnetic
alloys: metals mixed together, like steel and brass
solids, liquids and gases: does it flow, does it keep its shape?
natural and artificial materials and where they come from
sorting with a branching key (a database)
combining materials in layers so each does one job
measured tests repeated for reliable results
glass is a solid: the 'slow liquid' myth
light and materials: shadows, screens and Raman's light fingerprint
goals: By the end your child can sort materials as transparent, translucent or opaque, and explain why each is used where it is.
By the end your child can list properties of metals, test which materials are magnetic, and explain that not all metals are.
By the end your child can sort objects with a branching key and make their own key with yes-or-no questions.
By the end your child can tell a solid from a liquid and a gas, including tricky cases like sand and rice.
By the end your child can carry out a measured test three times and say whether the results are reliable.
By the end your child can explain why a good design often uses several materials, each for a different property.

lets some light through, but blurred, like butter paper or frosted glass
a material that is usually shiny, rings when struck, and lets heat and electricity pass through easily
attracted by a magnet. Iron, most kinds of steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic.
a mixture of a metal with other metals or carbon, like steel (iron and carbon) or brass (copper and zinc)
flows and takes the shape of its container, but keeps the same amount

a chart of yes-or-no questions that sorts things step by step

days.title: Understand my room
days.goal: Recall last year and map every material in one room.

steps.title: Remember Class 2
steps.do: Ask: 'What is the difference between a natural and a made material? Tell me how one made material is made.' (Glass is made by melting sand. Brick is made by baking clay.) 'How do you make a test fair?' (Change one thing, keep the rest the same, and measure.) 'Remember Stephanie Kwolek, the chemist whose cloudy liquid became Kevlar? What did she teach us?' (You can't tell what a material can do by looking at it. You have to test it.) Say: 'This year we test materials in harder ways.'

steps.title: Material map of my room
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Your child draws a simple map of the room they sleep in, seen from above, and labels every object they can. Then they tally the materials: wood, metal, plastic, glass, cloth, paper, stone or tile, and 'mixed' (more than one material). Ask: 'Which material is used most in your room? Why do you think that is?' (Often plastic or cloth, because they are cheap, light and easy to shape. In older homes, often wood.) 'Which things came from far away? Which came from nearby?'

steps.title: Where did it come from?
steps.do: Pick three things from the map and trace each one back together, as far as you can. A steel almirah: iron ore dug from hills in Karnataka, Odisha or Jharkhand, then melted with coal in a blast furnace. A cotton bedsheet: cotton fields, a spinning mill, then a weaver or a factory. A plastic bucket: oil from under the ground or the sea, then a chemical factory. Ask: 'Who are all the people in this object's journey?'

need: A3 paper or two A4 sheets taped together

days.title: Light through things
days.goal: Sort materials as transparent, translucent or opaque, and measure how much light gets through.

steps.title: How many layers to darkness?
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. First sort the materials. Hold each one between the torch and the wall. Your child says transparent (you see clearly through it), translucent (light comes through, but blurred) or opaque (no light comes through). Then measure. Hold one sheet of butter paper in front of the torch, then add sheets one at a time. Count how many sheets it takes until no light shows on the wall. Do the same with tissue paper and thin cotton cloth. Ask: 'Is translucent a fixed property, or does it depend on how thick the material is?' (It depends on thickness. One sheet is translucent, but many sheets together are opaque.)

steps.title: Why here?
steps.do: Ask: 'Why is bathroom window glass often frosted?' (It is translucent. Light comes in, but people outside can't see in.) 'Why are headlights transparent? Why is a pressure cooker opaque, and does it matter?' (It doesn't need to be see-through. It needs to be strong and carry heat to the food.) 'Why do some old houses, forts and temples have a jaali, a stone screen full of holes?' (Light and air come in, but the room stays private and cool.)

steps.title: Does old glass flow?
steps.do: Tell voice v2. Many people believe that old church windows in Europe are thicker at the bottom because glass is a very slow liquid that has dripped down over hundreds of years. Ask your child how they could check this. Then tell what scientists found. Ask: 'Why do you think a wrong idea can last so long?' Good answers: it sounds clever, people repeat it without checking, and the thick bottoms seemed to prove it.

need: 15 sheets of butter paper or tracing paper
a glass tumbler, plastic file sleeve, steel plate, cardboard, frosted glass if you have it

days.title: Shadows, screens and a fingerprint of light
days.goal: Use drama and dance to explore light through materials, and meet C.V. Raman and Kamala Sohonie.

steps.title: Shadow play
steps.do: Do Activity a3. Hang an old white bedsheet or veshti across a doorway and put a torch or lamp behind it. Your child makes shadow animals and acts a short story behind the screen while you watch from the front. A crow stealing a bangle works well. Ask: 'Why can I see your shadow but not your face?' (The sheet is translucent. It lets light through but scatters it. Your body is opaque and blocks the light.) Then change the screen. A clear plastic sheet gives no shadow picture, just a clear view. A thick blanket shows nothing at all. Ask: 'Which material makes the best shadow-puppet screen, and why?' Tell your child that in Kerala, tholpavakoothu shadow-puppet shows use a thin white cloth screen with oil lamps behind it.

steps.title: Clear, mist, hide: a dance
steps.do: Give your child three things to dance with: a thin chiffon dupatta or a clear plastic sheet (transparent), butter paper or a thin cotton towel (translucent), and a tray or a piece of cardboard (opaque). Play music. When you call 'CLEAR', they dance and look at you through the transparent one. When you call 'MIST', they dance behind the translucent one, so you see only a blurred shape. When you call 'HIDE', they hide behind the opaque one. Then they call and you dance. Afterwards ask: 'Is morning fog transparent, translucent or opaque?' (Translucent when it is thin, almost opaque when it is thick.)

steps.title: Raman's light, and Kamala Sohonie
steps.do: Tell voice v4. C.V. Raman was born near Tiruchirappalli in Tamil Nadu. In 1928, working in Calcutta, he found that when light passes through a transparent liquid, a tiny part of it comes out a slightly different colour. That change is different for each material, like a fingerprint. In 1930 he became the first Asian to win the Nobel Prize in Physics. A few years later, a young chemist named Kamala Sohonie applied to his institute in Bangalore. He refused her because she was a woman, and she would not accept that. Ask the voice's question. Then ask: 'Can a person be a great scientist and also be unfair? Can someone who was unfair change?' Let your child think. There is no neat answer.

need: an old white bedsheet or veshti, and a torch or lamp
a chiffon dupatta or clear plastic sheet, butter paper or a thin cotton towel, and a tray

days.title: Metals and magnets
days.goal: Find what makes a metal a metal, and discover which metals are magnetic.

steps.title: Knock, shine and touch
steps.do: Collect a steel spoon, a brass or copper vessel (a brass lamp or a copper tumbler), a ball of aluminium foil, an iron nail, a wooden spoon, a plastic spoon and a stone. Your child taps each one gently with a second steel spoon and listens. Metals ring, and we say they are sonorous. Wood and plastic thud. Next they rub each one to see if it shines. Last, leave everything in a cool place for a few minutes, then touch each with a fingertip. The metals feel colder, because they carry heat away from your finger quickly. Say: 'Metals are usually shiny, ring when struck, and carry heat and electricity well. That's why a pressure cooker is metal, and its handle is plastic.'

steps.title: Which materials are magnetic?
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. First your child predicts, for each object, whether a fridge magnet will attract it. To attract means to pull something towards itself. Then they test each object and sort it: magnetic or not magnetic. Be ready for a surprise. Many steel tumblers and plates are not magnetic, because there are different kinds of stainless steel. Ask: 'Is it true that all metals are magnetic?' (No. Aluminium, copper, brass, gold and silver are not. Iron, most steels, nickel and cobalt are.) Then teach the word alloy: a metal mixed with other metals or with carbon. Steel is iron with a little carbon. Stainless steel also has chromium, and sometimes nickel. Brass is copper mixed with zinc. Mixing changes the properties.

steps.title: Sort the scrap
steps.do: Ask: 'A scrap dealer gets a huge pile of mixed scrap metal. How could a magnet help?' (The magnet pulls out the iron and steel. What is left is aluminium, copper and brass, which sell for more.) Tell your child that scrap yards really do use giant electromagnets on cranes.

need: a steel spoon, brass or copper vessel, aluminium foil, iron nail, safety pin, paper clip, steel tumbler, wooden and plastic spoons, a stone, a key, a glass bangle

days.title: Solids, liquids and gases, and the branching key
days.goal: Sort by state of matter, including tricky cases, and sort objects with a key.

steps.title: Does it flow?
steps.do: Do Experiment e4. Pour water from a glass into a bowl, then into a bottle. It flows and takes the shape of each, but the amount stays the same. That makes it a liquid. Hold a stone. It keeps its shape, so it is a solid. Now pour rice or sand. It flows too! Ask: 'Is rice a liquid?' Let your child look at one grain. Each grain is a tiny solid that keeps its shape. The pile flows because the grains roll over each other. Then stuff a tissue into the bottom of a dry glass, turn the glass upside down and push it straight down into a bucket of water. Lift it straight out. The tissue is dry. Ask why. (The glass was full of air. Air is a gas. It takes up space, so it kept the water out.)

steps.title: Branching key
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Put 8 objects on the table: a steel spoon, a glass marble, a wooden block, a plastic ruler, a cotton hanky, a rubber band, a ball of aluminium foil and a sheet of paper. Your child asks a yes-or-no question that splits them into two groups, for example 'Is it magnetic?' Then they ask a new question for each group, such as 'Is it transparent?' or 'Is it flexible?' They keep going until each object is alone at the end of a branch. Draw it as a tree on a big sheet. Say: 'This is how scientists and computers sort huge numbers of things, one yes-or-no question at a time.' Then you secretly choose one object, and your child finds which one it is by asking the key's questions.

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1. For written items, ask for a full reason with 'because'.

need: a glass, a bowl, a bottle, water
a cup of rice or dry sand
a bucket of water and a tissue

days.title: The climbing water test
days.goal: Do a measured test three times and decide if results are reliable.

steps.title: Which paper drinks fastest?
steps.do: Do Experiment e3. Cut strips 2 cm wide and 15 cm long from four materials: paper towel, newspaper, printer paper and cotton cloth. Cut three strips of each, so you can test each material three times at once. Draw a line across each strip, 1 cm from the bottom, with a washable felt pen. Clip the strips to pencils laid across a tray of water, so the bottoms just touch the water. After 5 minutes, your child measures in centimetres how far the water has climbed, and writes it in the table.

steps.title: Are the results reliable?
steps.do: Look at the three numbers for each material. Ask: 'Are they close together or far apart?' If they are close, the result is reliable: you would get nearly the same answer again. If one is very different, ask: 'What might have gone wrong?' (The strip didn't touch the water, or it touched the side of the tray.) Then ask: 'Which material climbed highest? Which would make the best wick for an oil lamp? Which would make the best kitchen towel?' Explain wicking: water sticks to the fibres, so it creeps up the tiny gaps between them, even against gravity.

steps.title: The colours separate
steps.do: Look closely at the felt-pen line. Has the ink spread into different colours as the water climbed? Ask: 'What does that tell us about the ink?' (It was a mixture of colours, and the water carried some colours further than others.) Say: 'Scientists use this trick, called chromatography, to find what is in a mixture.'

need: paper towel, newspaper, printer paper, cotton cloth
a washable black or brown felt pen

days.title: Why a moon suit has many layers
days.goal: Understand why the best designs combine materials, each with a job.

steps.title: Story: The Twenty Skins
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Don't explain it. Ask: 'Why couldn't the suit be made of just one material?' Good answer: each layer had one job. One held the air in, one reflected the Sun's heat, one would not burn, and one was tough against sharp moon dust. Then ask: 'Whom did the TV show? Whom didn't it show?'

steps.title: The seamstresses
steps.do: Talk about voice v3 and ask its question. Point out that the women who sewed the suits had spent years sewing bras and girdles, and that skill turned out to be exactly what the Moon needed.

steps.title: Design a superhero suit
steps.do: Your child designs a suit, in layers, for a superhero who must visit four places. The Moon has no air, and is boiling hot in sunlight and freezing at night. The bottom of the Indian Ocean is dark and cold, and the water above presses hard enough to crush a car. The rim of a volcano has fierce heat and sharp rock. The top of Kangchenjunga has thin air and icy wind. For each place, your child writes what the suit must survive and which layer would do it. For example: an airtight inner layer holds air in on the Moon, a rigid shell resists the deep sea, shiny layers reflect heat, wool keeps out cold, and a tough outer layer stops sharp rock. They draw the suit with labels. Ask: 'Which two jobs fight each other?' (A rigid shell resists the squeeze of the deep sea but makes it hard to move. Thick warm layers are heavy.) 'Would you make one suit or four?'

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2, starting with the layers question in section C while the story is fresh. Then do the branching-key and climbing-water sections, using your Day 6 results table.

days.title: New materials, and the material trump cards
days.goal: Meet graphene and compare materials by their properties.

steps.title: Pencil and sticky tape
steps.do: Do Experiment e5. Your child scribbles a dark square on paper with a soft pencil (2B or darker), presses clear sticky tape on it, peels it off and sticks it on white paper. Then they press a fresh piece of tape onto the first tape and peel it apart, again and again. Look with a magnifying glass. Say: 'Pencil lead is graphite. It is made of layers of carbon stacked like the pages of a book. Each time you peel, you split the book into thinner pages.' Then tell voice v1: scientists did exactly this, many times over, until they got a layer just one atom thick. They called it graphene.

steps.title: Graphene and the Friday nights
steps.do: Discuss voice v1. Ask its question. Point out that the experiment started as a playful 'Friday night experiment', not a serious project.

steps.title: Material Trumps
steps.do: Play the card game g1. Each card is a material with scores for strength, bend (flexibility), see-through (transparency) and soaks (absorbency), and whether it is magnetic. When a player chooses a property, they must say why their material scores high or low on it.

steps.title: Start the building survey
steps.do: Begin the project: choose a building to survey (your home, a neighbour's, a temple, a shop). List its parts (walls, floor, roof, windows, doors, frames, pipes, wires) on a sheet with columns for MATERIAL and WHY.

days.title: The building survey, and teach it back
days.goal: Finish the survey, take on the challenge worksheet and explain the whole topic.

steps.title: Finish the building survey
steps.do: Finish the project. For each part of the building, your child writes the material, one property that makes it good for that job, and whether it is natural or made. Then they test what they can: tap pipes (metal or plastic?), try a magnet on a window grill and a door handle, check which windows are transparent or translucent. Ask: 'If you could change one material in this building, what would you change and why?'

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3. The last items have no single answer. Ask your child to defend their view with evidence.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child presents the building survey to the family. Then they explain five things: transparent, translucent and opaque, which materials are magnetic (and the steel tumbler surprise), how a branching key works, why the moon suit had many layers, and why old glass doesn't flow. Ask the check questions.

experiments.title: How many layers to darkness?
experiments.question: Is a material translucent or opaque, and does thickness matter?
need: a wall in a dim room
15 sheets of butter paper or tracing paper
a glass tumbler, a plastic file sleeve, a steel plate, cardboard
steps: Shine the torch on the wall.
Hold each material in front of it and sort: transparent, translucent or opaque.
Now hold one sheet of butter paper in front of the torch.
Add sheets one at a time, counting, until no light reaches the wall.
Repeat with tissue paper and thin cloth (fold it over and over).
Record the number of layers for each.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'How many sheets of butter paper will it take before the light disappears?'
experiments.observe: Transparent things make a bright spot. Translucent things make a blurry glow. Opaque things make a shadow. Each added layer dims the glow. If light still shows after 15 sheets, write '15 or more'.
experiments.why: Each layer of fibres scatters and absorbs a little light. One thin layer lets much of it through, scattered, so it is translucent. Enough layers stop it all, so the stack is opaque. So whether something is translucent depends partly on how thick it is, not only on what it is made of.
experiments.safety: Don't shine the torch into eyes.

experiments.title: Which materials are magnetic?
experiments.question: Are all metals magnetic?
need: an iron nail, a safety pin, a paper clip, a steel spoon, a steel tumbler or plate, aluminium foil, a brass or copper vessel, a key, a glass bangle, a wooden spoon, a plastic spoon, a stone
steps: Your child predicts magnetic or not for each object and writes it down.
Touch the magnet to each object.
Sort into magnetic and not magnetic.
Compare with predictions.
experiments.predict: Most children predict that all metals are magnetic. Write their predictions first.
experiments.observe: The nail, pin, paper clip and often the spoon stick. Aluminium, copper, brass, glass, wood, plastic and stone do not. Many stainless-steel tumblers and plates do not stick either.
experiments.why: Only a few metals are strongly magnetic: iron, nickel, cobalt and alloys containing them in the right form. Steel is mostly iron, so most steel is magnetic. But some stainless steels, used for kitchen vessels, contain nickel and chromium arranged so that the steel is hardly magnetic. Mixing metals into an alloy can change its properties completely.
experiments.safety: Keep magnets away from phones, cards and very small children, who might swallow small magnets.

experiments.title: The climbing water test
experiments.question: Which material soaks water upwards fastest?
need: strips 2 cm by 15 cm of paper towel, newspaper, printer paper and cotton cloth (three of each if possible)
steps: Draw a pen line 1 cm from the bottom of each strip.
Clip the strips to pencils laid across the tray, so each bottom just touches the water.
Start the timer. After 5 minutes, take the strips out.
Measure how far the water climbed, in centimetres.
Test three strips of each material, either all at once or one after another.
Write all results in a table and compare.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to rank the four materials from 'climbs highest' to 'climbs least'.
experiments.observe: The height of water on each strip, and how close the three tries are. Paper towel and cotton usually climb highest. Printer paper climbs least.
experiments.why: Water sticks to the fibres and to itself. In the narrow gaps between fibres, this draws water upwards against gravity. This is called wicking, or capillary action. Soft, fluffy materials with many fine gaps wick best. Testing three times shows whether the results are reliable.

experiments.title: Does it flow? Is the glass empty?
experiments.question: How can we tell solids, liquids and gases apart?
need: a glass of water, a bowl and a bottle
a cup of rice or dry sand
a dry glass and a tissue
steps: Pour the water into the bowl, then into the bottle. Notice the shape changes but the amount stays the same.
Hold the stone. Try to make it change shape.
Pour the rice. Then look at one grain with a magnifier.
Stuff a tissue into the bottom of a dry glass. Turn the glass upside down and push it straight down into the bucket. Lift it straight out.
Feel the tissue.
experiments.observe: Water takes the shape of each container. The stone keeps its shape. Rice flows, but each grain is a hard solid. The tissue stays dry.
experiments.why: Solids keep their shape. Liquids flow and take the shape of their container, but keep their volume. Gases spread out to fill any space. Rice and sand flow because they are many small solids rolling past each other. The upside-down glass was full of air. Air is a gas that takes up space, so the water could not get in.

experiments.title: Pencil and sticky tape
experiments.question: What is pencil lead made of, and can we split it?
steps: Scribble a dark square, about 3 cm across, on paper.
Press a strip of tape firmly onto it and peel it off.
Stick a fresh piece of tape onto the dark tape and peel it apart. Repeat several times.
Stick the tapes in order on white paper and compare how dark they are.
Look with the magnifying glass.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the grey get lighter each time? Can it go on for ever?'
experiments.observe: Each peel gives a lighter, thinner grey layer. Shiny flakes can be seen through a magnifier.
experiments.why: Pencil 'lead' is graphite: carbon atoms in flat sheets stacked like pages, held together only weakly. That's why it slides off onto paper. Each peel splits the stack thinner. In 2004 scientists at Manchester did this with better graphite and found flakes one atom thick: graphene, one of the strongest materials ever measured.

activities.title: Material map of my room
steps: Draw the room from above.
Label every object you can.
Tally the materials.
Mark things made of more than one material.
activities.outcome: A labelled map and a tally showing which materials your child lives among.

activities.title: Branching key
steps: Ask one yes-or-no question that splits the objects into two groups.
Ask a new question for each group.
Keep going until each object is alone.
Draw it as a tree.
Test it: hide an object and find it with the key.
activities.outcome: A branching key your child designed and tested.

activities.title: Shadow play
steps: Hang the sheet across a doorway with a light behind it.
Act a short story in shadows.
Try a transparent sheet and a thick blanket instead.
Decide which makes the best screen.
activities.outcome: A shadow play, and a clear sense of transparent, translucent and opaque.

project.title: Survey a building
steps: Choose a building: home, a temple, a shop or a neighbour's house.
List its parts: walls, floor, roof, windows, doors, frames, grills, pipes, wires, furniture.
For each part write the material and one property that makes it suitable.
Mark each material natural or made, and test what you can (tap, magnet, look through).
Find one part where you would choose a different material, and explain why.
Present it as a table or a labelled drawing.
project.outcome: A materials survey of a real building, with reasons, tests and one improvement.

game.title: Material Trumps
rules: Cut out the cards. Each shows a material and its scores out of 5 for strength, bend (flexibility), see-through (transparency) and soaks (absorbency), and whether it is magnetic.
Deal all the cards. Hold yours face up in a pile so you only see the top card.
The first player chooses one property from their top card, says it aloud, and must say WHY their material scores high or low ('Steel, strength 5, because it holds up bridges').
Everyone reads that property from their top card. The highest score wins all the top cards. For 'magnetic', a yes beats a no.
If two cards tie, put them in the middle. The next winner takes them too.
The player with all the cards, or the most after 15 minutes, wins.

Cotton cloth: strength 2, bend 5, see-through 1, soaks 5, magnetic no
Wool: strength 2, bend 5, see-through 0, soaks 4, magnetic no
Silk: strength 3, bend 5, see-through 1, soaks 3, magnetic no
cards.back: saris, such as Kanchipuram and Banarasi silk

cards.front: Paper: strength 1, bend 4, see-through 1, soaks 4, magnetic no
Paper towel: strength 1, bend 5, see-through 1, soaks 5, magnetic no
Plastic (bottle): strength 2, bend 3, see-through 4, soaks 0, magnetic no
Rubber: strength 2, bend 5, see-through 0, soaks 0, magnetic no
Stone (granite): strength 5, bend 0, see-through 0, soaks 1, magnetic no
Brick: strength 4, bend 0, see-through 0, soaks 3, magnetic no
Clay pot (terracotta): strength 2, bend 0, see-through 0, soaks 3, magnetic no
cards.back: water pots that keep water cool

cards.front: Iron: strength 5, bend 1, see-through 0, soaks 0, magnetic yes
Kevlar: strength 5, bend 4, see-through 0, soaks 1, magnetic no
Jute: strength 3, bend 4, see-through 0, soaks 4, magnetic no
Graphene: strength 5, bend 5, see-through 5, soaks 0, magnetic no
cards.back: still being tested for screens and batteries

big: Why do we notice the astronaut but not the people who sewed his suit?
If a wrong idea (like glass flowing) can last a hundred years, how many wrong ideas might we believe today?
Is it better to have one wonder material, or many ordinary materials working together?
Who should own a new material: the scientist who found it, the company that paid, or everyone?
Does a material have a 'job', or do we give it one?

challenge.q: Everyone 'knows' metals are magnetic. Are they?
challenge.hint: Only a few are: iron, nickel, cobalt and some of their alloys. Aluminium, copper, brass, gold and silver are not, and many stainless-steel kitchen vessels are hardly magnetic at all. Ask: what other 'everyone knows' facts could you test with something in your kitchen?

challenge.q: Old church windows are thicker at the bottom, so glass must be a slow liquid. True?
challenge.hint: No. Calculations (for example by Edgar Zanotto in 1998) show that window glass at room temperature would take far longer than the age of the universe to flow visibly. Old glass was made by spinning or blowing, which made uneven sheets, and builders often put the thicker edge at the bottom. Some old windows are thicker at the top or sides. Ask: what would you have needed to check, to catch this myth earlier?

challenge.q: Graphene was discovered with sticky tape on a Friday night. Do great discoveries need expensive equipment?
challenge.hint: Sometimes they do, but this one used tape, pencil-like graphite and a microscope, plus years of knowledge and the freedom to play. Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov won the Nobel Prize in 2010. Ask: what made it possible for them to play, and do all scientists get that freedom?

perspectives.who: The women of the ILC factory who sewed the Apollo moon suits
perspectives.view: They sewed layer after layer by hand and machine, so precisely that a small mistake could have cost a life. Ask: whose skill do we call 'science' and whose do we call 'just sewing'? Is that fair?
Thick walls of stone or mud and small windows, or stone jaalis, keep a house cool in a desert summer. Ask: why might a builder choose opaque, thick walls instead of big glass windows in Jaisalmer?
The iron in our almirahs and spoons was dug out of hills, often where Adivasi communities have lived for centuries. Ask: who should decide whether a hill is dug up for its iron?

Fish near the bottom of the ocean live under a pressure that would crush a submarine without a strong hull, and their soft bodies are fine, because they are full of water and pressed equally from inside and out. Ask: who is better designed for the deep sea, a fish or a human in a metal suit?

voices.who: Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov, University of Manchester, UK (2004)
voices.idea: During playful 'Friday night experiments', Geim's group used sticky tape to peel flakes of graphite thinner and thinner, until they found flakes just one atom thick: graphene. They showed it was a real, stable material with astonishing properties: very strong, flexible, almost transparent, and an excellent conductor.
voices.then: Many scientists had believed a sheet one atom thick could not exist on its own. They thought it would curl up or fall apart. Their first paper was rejected by a leading journal.
voices.now: Geim and Novoselov won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics. Graphene is now studied all over the world. Scientists still argue about how soon it will be used in everyday things.
voices.ask: Experts said a one-atom-thick sheet couldn't exist. What finally changed their minds: an argument or evidence?

voices.who: The 'glass is a slow liquid' myth, and scientists who tested it, such as Edgar Zanotto (Brazil, 1998)
voices.idea: For many years people claimed old window glass is thicker at the bottom because glass is a liquid that flows very, very slowly.
voices.then: The idea was repeated in classrooms and books for decades because it sounded clever and seemed to explain the uneven windows.
voices.now: Zanotto calculated that ordinary window glass at room temperature would take far longer than the age of the universe to sag visibly. The uneven panes come from old glassmaking methods, and they are not always thicker at the bottom. Glass is an amorphous solid: its particles are jumbled like a liquid's, but locked in place.
voices.ask: The myth had a real observation behind it (thick bottoms). What else could explain that observation? How would you test which explanation is right?

voices.who: The seamstresses of the International Latex Corporation (ILC), Dover, Delaware, USA (1960s)
voices.idea: The company, until then best known for making bras and girdles, won the job of making the Apollo moon suits. Its seamstresses, mostly women, sewed many layers of different materials, each with a job, to extremely exact measurements. Even pins were banned in case one pierced the airtight layer.
voices.then: Few people outside the factory knew their names. The suits were credited to the company and the engineers, and the astronauts became famous.
voices.now: Historians, for example Nicholas de Monchaux in his book 'Spacesuit: Fashioning Apollo', have written about how much the suits depended on the seamstresses' skill. Every suit that walked on the Moon worked.
voices.ask: Why do you think the skill of sewing was not seen as 'science'? What would have happened to the astronauts without it?

voices.who: C.V. Raman (1888–1970) and Kamala Sohonie (1911–1998), India
voices.idea: In 1928, at the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science in Calcutta, Raman (with K.S. Krishnan) found that when light passes through a transparent material, a tiny part of it is scattered with a slightly changed colour, and the change is different for each substance: a fingerprint. This is the Raman effect. He won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics.
voices.then: Raman was celebrated as proof that world-class science could be done in India, with modest equipment. Yet in 1933, as director of the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore, he refused to admit Kamala Sohonie as a research student because she was a woman. She protested and would not leave. He let her in, but on strict conditions. She did outstanding work, was later admitted to Cambridge, and in 1939 became one of the first Indian women to earn a PhD in a science.
voices.now: Raman spectroscopy is used everywhere today, from testing medicines to studying rocks on Mars. Sohonie's success is said to have helped open IISc to women in later years. Raman's colleague K.S. Krishnan, who did much of the experimental work, is less often remembered.
voices.ask: Raman showed that light reveals what a material really is. What did Kamala Sohonie reveal about Raman and his institute? Why do you think her name and Krishnan's are less known than his?

story.title: The Twenty Skins
text: My name is Ruth, and in the winter of 1968 I was sewing a man's skin.

Not his real skin, of course. His real skin was soft and pink like anyone's, and it would be inside. I was sewing the skins that would go around it: one after another, each one thin, each one different, so many that when they were finished, the suit would stand up on its own in the corner like a sleeping white giant.

Before that, I sewed girdles and bras. That's what our factory in Dover, Delaware, had always made. Then the space agency wanted a suit for walking on the Moon, and our company said: we know how to make soft things that hold a body tight and still let it move. Nobody laughed for long, because we were right.
On my first day in the space room, the supervisor gave me a pile of materials and said, 'Learn them like you'd learn people's faces.'

There was the rubber-coated cloth for the inside, smooth and a little sticky. That was the one that held the air in. On the Moon there is no air at all, and without that layer a man's blood would boil and his lungs would empty. It was the most important layer, and the weakest. A single pinprick would let the air out. That's why pins were forbidden in our room. We held layers together with our fingers and our patience.

Then there were the shiny layers, thin as a sweet wrapper, silver on one side. On the Moon, in sunlight, the ground can be hotter than boiling water. At night it is colder than anywhere on Earth. The shiny layers reflected the fierce sunlight away, and between them were thin gauzy layers to keep them from touching, because a gap of nothing at all is the best blanket there is.

There was a layer of tough cloth to stop sharp grains of moon dust from cutting through. And on the outside was the cloth they called Beta cloth, white and stiff, woven from threads of glass coated with something slippery. It would not burn.

That layer had come because of a fire. In January 1967, three astronauts had died on the launch pad when a fire broke out inside their capsule during a test. Afterwards, everything that could burn was changed. So the outermost skin was made of glass, woven so fine it felt like canvas. When I first held it I thought of my grandmother's glass bangles, and I could not believe that something so hard could become something so soft.

Altogether there were around twenty layers. I learned them all. Each was good at one thing and bad at others. The rubber held air but would melt in a fire. The shiny layers reflected heat but tore easily. The Beta cloth would not burn but cracked if folded too sharply. Not one material could do the whole job. Together, stitched in the right order, they could keep a man alive in a place that wanted him dead.

We measured to a fraction of a millimetre. If the stitch line wandered, the layer was thrown out and we started again. My friend Dot once worked eleven hours on a glove and found one stitch off by the width of a hair. She cut it all apart. Nobody told her to. She just thought about the hand that would be inside it.

On the night of 20 July 1969, I sat in my living room with my husband and my two boys and watched a grey, fuzzy television. A white shape came slowly down a ladder onto the Moon. My boys shouted. My husband cried a little, though he says he didn't.

The man on the television was famous by morning. Everyone knew his name. Nobody on the television said my name, or Dot's, or the names of any of the women in that room in Dover. I didn't mind, at first.

But I sat there in the dark and I thought: inside that suit there is rubber that came from a tree, and glass that came from sand, and plastic that came from oil under the ground, and nylon thread that a woman's hands pulled through, stitch by stitch. He is standing on the Moon wrapped in the whole Earth, and in us.
I watched him take a step. I watched the white knee bend, and I knew exactly which seam was bending, and who had sewn it.
story.epiphany: No single material can do every job. The best designs combine materials, each chosen for one property (holding air, reflecting heat, not burning, resisting cuts). The turn is Ruth's realisation that 'not one material could do the whole job', and at the end that the suit is 'the whole Earth' in layers. Underneath: the skilled women whose work made it possible but whose names were not on the television. Based on real history: ILC's seamstresses sewed the Apollo suits, pins were banned, and the fireproof Beta cloth came after the Apollo 1 fire. Ruth and Dot are imagined characters.
ask: Name three layers of the suit and the job each one did.
Why were pins not allowed in the sewing room?
Why did the outermost layer have to be fireproof?
What did Ruth mean when she said the astronaut was 'wrapped in the whole Earth'?
Who do you think should be remembered for walking on the Moon?

ideas.more: A suit, a house, a pressure cooker with a plastic handle: each part is a different material with a different property. Engineers ask what each part needs to do.

ideas.idea: Properties can be surprising, so we test instead of assuming.
ideas.more: Not all metals are magnetic. A steel tumbler may not stick to a magnet. Glass is a solid. Rice flows. Anything that 'everyone knows' can be tested.

ideas.idea: Every material connects us to a place and to people.
ideas.more: Iron from hills in Karnataka or Jharkhand, cotton from fields in Telangana or Gujarat, rubber from Kerala, oil from under the sea. Every object in your room came from somewhere on Earth and passed through many people's hands.

unknowns: What exactly is glass? Its particles are jumbled like a liquid's but stuck like a solid's, and physicists still argue about how best to explain why liquids become glass when they cool. Some call it one of the deepest unsolved problems in the physics of solids.
Will graphene change everyday life, as some predicted, or stay mostly in laboratories? Nobody knows yet. Making it cheaply in large, perfect sheets is still hard.

Why are only a few metals, like iron, nickel and cobalt, strongly magnetic? Scientists can explain it with the physics of electrons, but predicting exactly which new alloys will be magnetic is still difficult.

check.q: What is the difference between transparent, translucent and opaque? Give an example of each.
check.a: Transparent lets light through clearly, like window glass. Translucent lets blurred light through, like butter paper or frosted glass. Opaque lets no light through, like steel or cardboard.

check.q: Are all metals magnetic? Give examples.
check.a: No. Iron, most steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic. Aluminium, copper, brass, gold, silver and some stainless steels are not.

check.q: What is an alloy? Name one.
check.a: A metal mixed with other metals or carbon: steel (iron and carbon), brass (copper and zinc), bronze (copper and tin).

check.q: Rice can be poured. Is it a liquid?
check.a: No. Each grain is a solid that keeps its shape. The pile flows because the grains roll over each other.

check.q: How does a branching key work?
check.a: You ask yes-or-no questions about properties, one at a time, splitting the group until each object is on its own.

check.q: How did we know our climbing water results were reliable?
check.a: We repeated the test three times and the results were close together.

check.q: Why did the moon suit need about twenty layers?
check.a: Each material did one job: holding air, reflecting heat, not burning, resisting cuts. No single material could do them all.
No. It is an amorphous solid, which means its particles are jumbled but locked in place. Old windows are uneven because of how the glass was made.
